title: Why do big ticket sales crash?

scenes.heading: Why do big *ticket sales* crash?
scenes.narration: In 2022, a huge tour's presale overwhelmed the ticket site. Why do big sales crash, and how do you design one that doesn't?

scenes.title: Everyone at once
scenes.narration: Everybody arrives in the same minute, fans and bots, hitting refresh. The backend runs out of capacity, and the database drowns in checks for the same seats.

scenes.title: The waiting room
scenes.narration: You can add servers, but not seats. So put a waiting room in front: at the start, everyone gets a random place in line, so refreshing doesn't help, and you let people in at the rate the database can handle. The price: some fans wait.

scenes.caption: total system requests · 2022 presale · 4× its previous peak (Ticketmaster)
scenes.narration: How big was it? The company reported three and a half billion requests in total, four times its previous peak, bots included. A waiting room turns it into a line.

scenes.title: Line them up
scenes.narration: Scale what you can, and line up what you can't. Random line, or first come, first served?

notes: Ticketmaster's explanation (Nov 19, 2022) of the Eras Tour Verified Fan onsale (Nov 15): "3.5 billion total system requests – 4x our previous peak", a "staggering" number of bot attacks plus fans without codes, about 15% of interactions with issues. It is a total with no period given, not a rate.

Scaling out works for the reads (copies behind a load balancer, the seat map on a CDN). The seats are the bottleneck: every purchase ends in the same rows of the same database, so more servers do not help.

Virtual waiting rooms (for example Queue-it): over-capacity visitors wait on a separate page; for scheduled sales, early visitors are randomized at the start; people are let in at a configured rate. A line is predictable and random order removes the advantage of arriving first; error pages would be random and reward whoever retries fastest, often bots.
The dots and the meters are pictures of magnitude, not measurements. The price of the waiting room: some fans wait, and the room itself becomes a target.
